description: Disease, forced labour and Christianisation in Mexico — and how silver inflated Europe.
content_html:
The Scale of Indigenous Depopulation

The most catastrophic consequence of the Spanish conquest was demographic. Before the Europeans arrived, the population of central Mexico is estimated by historians at somewhere between five and thirty million people — the wide range reflects the difficulty of calculating pre-contact populations. Within a century of contact, that population had collapsed by an estimated 50–90 per cent, primarily from epidemic disease. Smallpox arrived in 1520; subsequent waves of measles, typhus, influenza and other diseases, to which indigenous people had no immune resistance, killed millions. One estimate suggests the central Mexican population fell from approximately 25 million in 1519 to around one million by 1600 — though these figures are contested among historians.

Key Fact

The indigenous population of central Mexico fell by an estimated 50–90 per cent within a century of Spanish contact, primarily from epidemic disease. Because indigenous peoples had no prior exposure to European diseases such as smallpox, measles and typhus, their immune systems offered no resistance — a “virgin soil epidemic.”

The Treatment of Indigenous Peoples: Encomienda and Forced Labour

The Spanish organised indigenous labour through the encomienda system. Each Spanish settler (encomendero) was allocated a group of indigenous people from whom they could demand tribute and labour. In theory, the encomendero was obliged to protect and Christianise their workers. In practice, it was forced labour under threat of violence, and conditions on encomiendas — particularly on agricultural estates and in mines — were brutal.

Mining was especially deadly. The silver mines of Potosí (in modern Bolivia, opened 1545) and other sites across New Spain used the mita — a rotating forced labour draft in which indigenous communities were required to supply a proportion of their men to work in mines for fixed periods. Conditions in the silver mines were lethal: men worked in near-darkness, inhaling toxic mercury vapour used in silver processing, with minimal food and no safety equipment. Life expectancy for mine workers was drastically shortened. The silver that flowed out of Potosí to Spain came at an enormous cost in indigenous lives.

Bartolomé de las Casas was a Spanish priest who had himself held an encomienda in the Caribbean before undergoing a dramatic change of conscience around 1514. He spent the rest of his life campaigning for indigenous rights, writing vivid accounts of Spanish atrocities and petitioning the Spanish crown to reform the colonial system. His most influential work, the Brevísima relación de la destrucción de las Indias (A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies, 1542), was translated into multiple languages and used by Spain’s Protestant rivals as evidence of Spanish cruelty — contributing to the “Black Legend” of Spanish colonial brutality. Las Casas’s advocacy contributed to the New Laws of 1542, which attempted (with limited success) to restrict encomienda abuses. He remains a deeply contested figure: praised as an early human rights defender, criticised for suggesting that enslaved Africans could replace indigenous labour.

The Imposition of Christianity

Christianity was imposed on indigenous populations throughout New Spain. Spanish missionaries — particularly Franciscan, Dominican and Augustinian friars — established missions across Mexico, teaching Christian doctrine, baptising converts and destroying indigenous religious sites and objects. The Templo Mayor in Mexico City was demolished; its stones used to build the new cathedral. Most Aztec codices were burned by Bishop Juan de Zumárraga and other churchmen who viewed them as works of the devil. Temples were torn down and churches built in their place, often on the same foundations.

The cultural impact was enormous. Indigenous religious practices did not disappear but went underground or blended with Christianity to create syncretic forms of worship. The syncretism also reshaped the Americas culturally: Spanish language, Catholic religion, European agricultural practices and livestock (horses, cattle, pigs) all transformed indigenous societies within a generation.

Key Fact

Spanish missionaries destroyed most Aztec codices and demolished indigenous temples, building Christian churches on the same foundations. The Aztec Templo Mayor in Mexico City was demolished and its stones used to build the new Spanish cathedral.

The Columbian Exchange and European Impact

The conquest initiated the Columbian Exchange — a vast transfer of goods, crops, animals and diseases in both directions across the Atlantic. From the Americas to Europe came maize, potatoes, tomatoes, chilli peppers, cacao and tobacco. These crops transformed European and global diets. From Europe to the Americas came wheat, cattle, horses, sugar cane, diseases and enslaved Africans.

The most dramatic European economic consequence was the Price Revolution: a sustained period of inflation across Europe during the sixteenth century. Spanish silver from the Americas — particularly from Potosí — flooded into European circulation, increasing the money supply and driving up prices. Wages lagged behind prices, impoverishing workers and peasants. Historians debate how much of the Price Revolution was caused by American silver versus other factors, but the connection is well established. Spain itself was paradoxically weakened by its silver wealth: easy money reduced incentives for domestic industry, and by the late sixteenth century Spain was using silver to pay for imports rather than building its own manufacturing base.

The conquest opened new trade routes and created new commodities. Cacao (chocolate) was initially used as currency in the Aztec empire and was introduced to Europe in the sixteenth century; by the seventeenth century it had become a luxury drink across Europe. Tobacco, also from the Americas, transformed European social habits. Sugar, grown in the Caribbean with enslaved African labour (as indigenous populations collapsed), became one of the most profitable commodities of the early modern period. The Atlantic economy — linking Europe, Africa and the Americas in a triangular trade — was a direct consequence of the voyages that began with Columbus in 1492.
exam_tip_html: For the 16-mark period essay, you must reach a substantiated overall judgement — not just describe two sides. For a question about the impact of the Spanish conquest, weigh the relative significance of different consequences: was disease or forced labour more damaging for indigenous peoples? Was the wealth Spain gained or the price inflation it triggered more significant for Europe? Always link your evidence explicitly to the question. For 8-mark “Explain Change” questions, be specific about what changed and for whom — a vague statement that “everything changed” scores poorly.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The indigenous population of central Mexico fell by an estimated 50–90 per cent within a century of contact, primarily from epidemic disease; the encomienda system and silver mining further devastated survivors through brutal forced labour.
  • Christianity was imposed by Spanish missionaries who destroyed codices and temples, building churches on indigenous sacred sites; cultural practices blended into syncretic forms that survived despite official suppression.
  • The Columbian Exchange transferred crops, animals, diseases and people between the hemispheres; the influx of American silver (especially from Potosí) caused the European Price Revolution of the sixteenth century, raising prices and impoverishing workers across the continent.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the encomienda system in New Spain.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying a feature (e.g. Spanish settlers were allocated the right to demand labour and tribute from a group of indigenous people / in theory they were to Christianise and protect workers; in practice it was forced labour / encomiendas were used in agriculture and mining). Two marks for a developed explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Columbian Exchange.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Food crops transferred from the Americas to Europe: maize, potatoes, tomatoes, chilli peppers, cacao, tobacco — transforming European diets.
• European crops, animals and diseases transferred to the Americas: wheat, cattle, horses, sugar cane, smallpox, measles — devastating indigenous populations.
• The transfer created a new Atlantic trading economy linking Europe, Africa and the Americas.
• The Columbian Exchange is named by historian Alfred Crosby and is seen as one of the most significant ecological events in human history.
[2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the European Price Revolution in the sixteenth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies the influx of American silver (particularly from Potosí, opened 1545) into European circulation as a cause; explains the mechanism — increased money supply exceeded growth in goods, so prices rose; links specifically to the Spanish silver trade and its impact on wages and prices across Europe.
Secure: Identifies a cause with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Names a cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague statement without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the imposition of Christianity on indigenous peoples of New Spain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains the destruction of indigenous cultural heritage (codices burned, temples demolished, churches built on sacred sites); or the creation of syncretic religious practices as indigenous beliefs blended with Catholic Christianity; develops with specific evidence (Bishop Zumárraga burning codices; Templo Mayor replaced by cathedral).
Secure: Identifies consequence with supporting evidence.
Developing: States a consequence with basic explanation.
Emerging: Brief point without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Bartolomé de las Casas for the history of the Spanish conquest.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses significance at the time (documented Spanish atrocities; petitioned the crown; contributed to New Laws of 1542 restricting encomienda abuses; former encomendero giving testimony unusual credibility) AND over time (his Brief Account became one of the most influential texts challenging colonialism; contributed to the Black Legend; cited by later human rights campaigners). Developed with evidence.
Secure: Addresses significance with evidence; may lack full over-time analysis.
Developing: Describes what Las Casas did without fully analysing significance.
Emerging: Brief or general points only.

practice_questions.text: 'Disease was a more significant consequence of the Spanish conquest than the imposition of Christianity for the peoples of central Mexico.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the interpretation:
• Disease caused a population collapse of 50–90% — the largest demographic catastrophe in the history of the Americas.
• Unlike cultural suppression, death was irreversible; the loss of people also weakened indigenous capacity to resist or maintain cultural practices.
• Disease spread independently of individual Spanish actions, killing millions before missionaries arrived.

Arguments challenging the interpretation:
• The imposition of Christianity destroyed codices, temples and religious knowledge that could never be recovered.
• Forced labour (encomienda and mita) directly killed people through overwork, particularly in silver mining.
• The Christianisation created a permanent cultural rupture; religious syncretism shows indigenous people resisting, but the original practices were suppressed and distorted.

Mastering: Sustained argument, agrees AND disagrees with evidence, reaches substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some relevant points, limited judgement.
Emerging: Descriptive, no evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: The silver mines of _____ in modern Bolivia became the largest silver-producing site in the Americas after 1545.
Bartolomé de las Casas was a Spanish _____ who became the most prominent advocate for indigenous rights in the Spanish Empire.
Match each consequence of the conquest to the group it most directly affected:
right: Indigenous population of central Mexico — killed 50–90% within a century
European workers and peasants — wages lagged behind rising prices
Indigenous labourers — forced to work on estates and in mines

flashcard_questions.q: What term describes the epidemic devastation caused by diseases arriving in a population with no prior exposure?

flashcard_questions.a: A colonial labour system granting Spanish settlers the right to demand labour and tribute from allocated indigenous people.

flashcard_questions.q: When were the silver mines of Potosí opened?
Who was Bartolomé de las Casas?
flashcard_questions.a: A Spanish Dominican friar who documented Spanish atrocities and campaigned for indigenous rights in the sixteenth century.

flashcard_questions.q: What was Las Casas's most influential work, published in 1542?
flashcard_questions.a: A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies (Brevísima relación de la destrucción de las Indias).
The transfer of plants, animals, diseases and people between eastern and western hemispheres after Columbus's 1492 voyage.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two crops that the Columbian Exchange brought from the Americas to Europe.
flashcard_questions.a: Any two from: maize, potatoes, tomatoes, chilli peppers, cacao, tobacco.

flashcard_questions.q: What caused the European Price Revolution of the sixteenth century?
flashcard_questions.a: Partly the influx of American silver, which increased the money supply and drove up prices.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened to most Aztec codices after the Spanish conquest?
flashcard_questions.a: They were destroyed by Spanish missionaries, particularly Bishop Juan de Zumárraga, who saw them as works of the devil.

flashcard_questions.q: What was built on the site of the Aztec Templo Mayor in Mexico City?
flashcard_questions.a: The Spanish cathedral, using Aztec stones — a deliberate act of religious and cultural erasure.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'syncretism' mean in the context of religion in New Spain?
flashcard_questions.a: The blending of indigenous Mesoamerican beliefs with Catholic Christianity, creating hybrid forms of worship.

glossary_terms.definition: A labour system in Spanish colonial America in which a settler was granted the right to demand labour and tribute from a group of indigenous people in exchange for a duty to protect and Christianise them.
A mining city in modern Bolivia, founded in 1545, which became the largest silver-producing site in the Americas and relied on indigenous forced labour.
Spanish Dominican friar (1484–1566) who became the most prominent advocate for indigenous rights, documenting Spanish atrocities in his 'Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies' (1542).
The transfer of plants, animals, diseases, people and ideas between the eastern and western hemispheres that followed Columbus's 1492 voyage.
The dramatic rise in prices across Europe during the sixteenth century, partly caused by the influx of silver from the Americas increasing the money supply.
The blending of indigenous Mesoamerican religious beliefs and practices with Catholic Christianity, producing hybrid forms of worship that survive in Mexico to the present day.
